The Chemical Structure of a DNA Polynucleotide

Text description of this image

DNA double helix: The DNA double helix resembles a twisted ladder. The rungs, split down the middle, are made up of pairs of letters (bases); A pairs with T and C pairs with G. Dotted lines join the pairs.; Polynucleotide: An exploded image of one section of DNA backbone with its attached bases shows the polynucleotide, represented with symbols. The backbone consists of repeating phosphates (short gold bands) and sugars (wide blue bands); bases extend from the sugars. The sequence of bases attached to the backbone in this drawing is A, C, T, G, and G. A and G are larger bases than C and T; this is represented here by making these bases twice as long.; Sugar-phosphate backbone: An image shows the sugar-phosphate backbone representing the phosphate groups as gold circles attached to blue pentagon sugars. Each sugar is attached to a nitrogenous base. The nitrogenous bases are drawn as rings; A and G are drawn as double-ring structures (a pentagon fused to a hexagon), while C and T are drawn as single ring structures (both are hexagons).; DNA molecule: An exploded image of one DNA nucleotide shows the chemical structures of the phosphate group, sugar (deoxyribose), and the base (here, thymine or T). The phosphate is attached to the sugar, which is attached to thymine. The sugar contains five carbons; all of them are highlighted. Four carbons are in corners of the pentagon ring; the fifth is attached above the ring. In detail, the structures in the nucleotide are as follows:; The phosphate group is a central P bonded to Os at the left, right, above, and below. The bond to the O on the left is a double bond; all other bonds are single bonds. The O below the central P has a negative charge; an open-ended line above the top O indicates that this will be the point of connection to the next nucleotide in the strand. From the O on the right of the P there is a single bond to CH2; the C in this CH2 is attached above the sugar ring and is one of the five carbons highlighted in deoxyribose sugar.; Deoxyribose sugar is a five-membered ring, with an O as the point of the pentagon at the top of the ring. All carbons in the sugar are highlighted. The carbon in the upper left corner is bonded to an H below the ring, and to CH2 above the ring; it is this CH2 that is bonded to the phosphate group as described previously. The carbon in the lower left corner is single-bonded to H above and to O below the ring; an open line below this O indicates that this is the point of connection to the next nucleotide in the strand. The carbon in the lower right corner is single-bonded to Hs above and below the ring. The carbon in the upper right corner is single-bonded to thymine off the ring, and to an H below the ring.; Thymine (T) is a single-ring structure. It is drawn as a hexagon with the points arranged vertically. There is a double bond in the left side of the ring; all other bonds within the ring are single bonds. At the bottom point of the ring is an N; this N is attached to the carbon in the upper right corner of the sugar as described previously. In the lower left corner of thymine is a C that is single-bonded to H. In the upper left corner is a C that is single-bonded to CH3. From the top carbon in the ring is a double bond to O above. In the upper right corner of the ring is an N that is single-bonded to H off the ring. The carbon in the lower right corner of the ring is double-bonded to O.

A Rope-Ladder Model of a Double Helix

Three Representations of DNA

Text description of this image

Figure (a) The figure shows that the sugar-phosphate backbones are blue ribbons, and the bases are complementary shapes in shades of green and orange. The DNA double helix resembles a twisted ladder with the backbone consisting of repeating phosphates (short gold bands) and sugars (wide blue bands); the bases extend inward from the sugars. Longer rungs (A and G) pair with shorter rungs (T and C); A pairs with T, and C with G. Dashed lines connect the bases (rungs); these are hydrogen bonds. Figure (b) The figure shows a chemically detailed structure of DNA with individual hydrogen bonds depicted by dashed lines. The sugars on the two strands are upside-down with respect to each other. DNA is composed of two strands joined together by hydrogen bonds between their bases. Each strand has a sugar-phosphate backbone; attached to each sugar is one base. A and G are double-ringed bases and C and T are single-ringed bases. Two hydrogen bonds join A and T; three hydrogen bonds form between C and G. On the left strand, phosphate groups attach to pentagon sugars; the point of the pentagons (an O) face up. The top component of the backbone of the left strand is a phosphate group; at the bottom of the strand (four nucleotides are drawn) is a sugar. Bases attach to the sugars in the example sequence (from top to bottom) A, G, T, and C. On the right strand the backbone arrangement is reversed; the top component of the backbone of the strand is a sugar and the bottom component is a phosphate group. The pentagon sugars on the right strand are upside-down, so that their point (the O) faces downward. The bases attached to the sugars are T, C, A, and G. In the specific structure of the phosphate groups, these are central P atoms joined on four sides to O (one has a negative charge). One O in each phosphate group is attached to the CH2 off the ring in the deoxyribose sugar. On the left strand this CH2 is above the ring; but because the sugars in the right strand are upside down, the CH2 on the right strand is below the ring. The bases are attached to the upper right corner of the sugar ring on the left strand; on the right strand the bases are attached to the lower left corner of the ring as oriented. Figure (c) A figure shows a computer model of DNA. Each atom is shown as a sphere, creating a space-filling model. Sugars and phosphates alternate at the edges of the molecule; the bases are joined in the center.

DNA Replication

Text description of this image

The figure shows the parental DNA molecule to be unwound at one end by breaking the hydrogen bonds between base pairs and separating them. The free strands then serve as the templates for two new daughter DNA strands, which form by adding new base pairs onto the parental DNA template (T is added to pair with A and C is added to pair with G). The two new daughter DNA molecules (double helices) will thus consist of half parental DNA and half new daughter DNA.

Multiple “Bubbles” in Replicating DNA

Text description of this image

The figure shows that origins of replication labeled on a segment of parental double stranded DNA. Exploded drawings of the regions surrounding these segments show the replication bubbles, which are bulging, opened regions of the DNA with the two parental strands on the outsides of the bubbles. The origin of replication is at the center of the bubbles. In each bubble, replication proceeds outward in both directions from the origin, building the daughter strands on the insides of the bubbles using the parental strands. Two daughter DNA molecules are produced.

The Flow of Genetic Information in a Eukaryotic Cell

Text description of this image

A figure shows an exploded view of part of the nucleus and surrounding cytoplasm of a eukaryotic cell. Transcription of the DNA takes place in the nucleus and produces RNA. Translation of the RNA takes place in the cytoplasm and produces a protein.

Transcription of DNA and Translation of Codons

Text description of this image

The figure shows a double-stranded DNA molecule with three sections labeled gene 1, gene 2, and gene 3. An exploded drawing of a small section of gene 3 shows the sequence of bases in one DNA strand. Transcription of the DNA produces RNA. Translation of each codon, or three-base sequence in the RNA, results in the addition of one amino acid for each codon. A string of amino acids is a polypeptide. The sequences shown are as follows:

DNA strand bases: AAA CCG GCA AAA; mRNA codons: UUU GGC CGU UUU; Polypeptide: Amino acid 1; Amino acid 2; Amino acid 3; Amino acid 1

Transcription

Text description of this image

The figure a shows an unwound section of the DNA molecule within an RNA polymerase. The bottom strand is used as the template strand, while the top strand is not used. RNA nucleotides are added to the right side of the template following base pairing rules; newly made RNA dangles from the left side of the polymerase. The nucleotides added here are as follows:

DNA template bases: T A G G T T; RNA nucleotides added: A U C C A A and The figure b shows the following steps:; Initiation: RNA polymerase attaches to the promoter region of the DNA of a gene. At the opposite end of the gene is the terminator DNA.; Elongation: As the RNA polymerase moves along the gene from the promoter toward the terminator, the RNA strand grows. The DNA unwinds in the polymerase and rewinds behind it.; Termination: The RNA polymerase reaches the terminator DNA and detaches from the DNA, as does the completed RNA strand.

The Production of Messenger RNA (mRNA) in a Eukaryotic Cell

Text description of this image

The figure shows that inside the nucleus, a DNA molecule consists of alternating regions of exons and introns. An RNA transcript is made from this DNA molecule, and a cap and tail are added to the ends. Next, the introns are removed from the RNA transcript, and the exons are spliced together. The mRNA molecule consists of the coding sequence (the spliced exons) with a cap at one end and tail at the other. The mRNA then exits the nucleus and enters the cytoplasm.

A Molecule of mRNA

Text description of this image

The figure shows an mRNA strand, with the cap at the tip, followed by a brief nucleotide sequence that is not part of the genetic message depicted as a pink section. It is then followed by the start of the genetic message. At the end of the strand is another pink section that comes after the end of the genetic message, followed by the tail on the tip.

The Ribosome

Text description of this image

The figure a shows a ribosome with a dome-shaped large subunit above a flattened small subunit. The mRNA binding site is shown between the two. The tRNA binding sites are slots in the large subunit, P site is shown on the left, and A site is shown on the right and The figure b shows a ribosome with two RNAs in the binding sites in the large subunit, with their anticodons bound to codons in the mRNA. The growing polypeptide chain extends from the tRNA in the P site on the left. The next amino acid to be added to the polypeptide is attached to the tRNA in the A site on the right.

The Structure of tRNA

Text description of this image

The figure shows that tRNA polynucleotide (ribbon model) consists of an RNA polynucleotide chain that twists and folds back, roughly forming the shape of T. A triplet set of bases called the anticodon is shown at one end and the amino acid attachment site is shown at the opposite end. A simplified representation of tRNA shows a column with the triplet anticodon at the bottom and a wick-like extension that is the amino acid attachment site at the opposite end of the structure.

The Elongation of a Polypeptide

Text description of this image

1. Codon recognition: Drawing of the ribosome with the mRNA bound between the large and small subunits. A tRNA is in the P site (on the left) of the large ribosomal subunit; the polypeptide extends from this tRNA. Its anticodon is bound to a codon on the mRNA. An incoming tRNA will enter the A site (on the right) of the large ribosomal subunit; its anticodon will bind to the mRNA codon at that site. The incoming tRNA carries an amino acid. 2. Peptide bond formation: A peptide bond forms between the amino acid carried by the tRNA in the A site and the amino acid on the polypeptide chain directly attached to the tRNA in the P site. 3. Translocation: After the new peptide bond forms, the polypeptide is attached to the tRNA in the A site. The tRNA in the P site (without an amino acid) leaves, and the mRNA shifts to the left, such that a new codon will be in the A site and the tRNA carrying the polypeptide chain will be in the P site. It is followed by step 1 starting again.

A Summary of Transcription and Translation

Text description of this image

1. Transcription: RNA is made on a DNA template. The figure shows the nucleus and DNA. RNA polymerase is attached to an unwound section of DNA and an mRNA is being transcribed from a template DNA strand. 2. RNA processing: The RNA transcript is spliced and modified to produce mRNA, which moves to the cytoplasm. Introns (pink, non-genetic message regions) are removed from the mRNA, and a cap and tail added to the ends of the mRNA strand. After processing the mRNA exits the nucleus. 3. Amino acid attachment: The tRNA molecules pick up their amino acids. The figure shows an amino acid being added to a tRNA with the help of an enzyme and ATP. At the opposite end of the amino acid is the tRNA’s anticodon (a 3-base sequence). 4. Initiation of translation: The first tRNA combines with the mRNA and ribosomal subunits to start polypeptide synthesis. The figure shows a tRNA in the P site of the large ribosomal subunit with its anticodon bound to a codon in the mRNA (the mRNA is bound to the small ribosomal subunit below). To the right of the P site in the large ribosomal subunit is the empty A site. 5. Elongation: The polypeptide elongates as amino acids are added. The figure shows a tRNA in the P site with an attached polypeptide chain. An incoming tRNA, carrying an amino acid, is entering the A site where its anticodon will bind to the corresponding codon in the mRNA. 6. Termination: A stop codon signals release of the completed polypeptide and separation of ribosomal units.

Mutations and Diversity

Three Types of Mutations and their Effects

Text description of this image

Normal gene: DNA TACTTCAAACCGCGT is transcribed to mRNA AUG AAG UUU GGC GCA, which codes for Met, Lys, Phe, Gly, Ala. (a) Base substitution: one nucleotide in the mRNA changes, so the fourth amino acid becomes Ser. The sequence is Met, Lys, Phe, Ser, Ala. (b) Nucleotide deletion: one nucleotide is deleted, which shifts the reading frame. The sequence is Met, Lys, Leu, Ala. (c) Nucleotide insertion: a G is inserted, which shifts the reading frame. The sequence is Met, Lys, Leu, Trp, Arg.

Bacteriophages (Viruses) Infecting a Bacterial Cell

Text description of this image

A colorized micrograph at a magnification of 225,000 shows three bacteriophages on a bacterial cell; each is about 200 nanometers tall and consists of a head, tail, and bending “legs.” The DNA of the viruses is being injected into the bacterial cell.

Alternative Phage Reproductive Cycles

Text description of this image

1. Phage attaches to cell. The diagram shows a phage attaching to a bacterial cell, which contains a large, round bacterial chromosome (DNA). The phage injects its DNA into the bacterial cell. 2. Phage DNA circularizes. The diagram shows a bacterial cell with a small circle of DNA and a larger one. Either step 3 (enters the lytic cycle) or step 5 (enters the lysogenic cycle) follows. 3. Lytic cycle. New phage DNA and proteins are synthesized. The diagram shows a bacterial cell containing phage DNA and proteins. Phages assemble from these components within the bacterial cell. 4. Lytic cycle. Cell lyses, releasing phages. Newly released phages may infect another cell (beginning the cycle again at step 1). 5. Lysogenic cycle. Phage DNA is inserted into the bacterial chromosome. The diagram shows a bacterial cell containing a circular prophage inserted into the bacterial chromosome. 6. Lysogenic cycle. Lysogenic bacterium reproduces normally, replicating the prophage at each cell division. 7. Lysogenic cycle. Occasionally a prophage may leave the bacterial chromosome. The diagram shows a bacterial cell with a small circular piece of DNA and a larger one. It is followed by step 2 starting again.

A figure shows a photo of a tobacco leaf mottled with tobacco mosaic disease, with a drawing of the tobacco mosaic virus that causes the disease. The rod-shape virus consists of RNA wrapped in a protein coat.

An Influenza Virus

Text description of this image

A figure shows an influenza virus, which consists of a membranous envelope covered in protein spikes surrounding eight molecules of RNA, each individually wrapped in a protein coat.

The Reproductive Cycle of an Enveloped Virus

Text description of this image

The figure shows virus attaching to the plasma membrane of a host cell. The virus is surrounded by protein spikes protruding from the viral envelope. Within the envelope, the viral RNA (genome) is wrapped in a protein coat. The figure shows the following steps: 1. Entry: The virus enters the host cell, merging its envelope with the plasma membrane of the host. 2. Uncoating: The viral RNA (genome) loses its protein coat and is exposed. 3. RNA synthesis by viral enzyme. RNA is synthesized from the viral RNA template. Step 3 branches to steps 4 and 5. 4. Protein synthesis: New viral proteins are made from the mRNA produced by viral enzymes. 5. RNA synthesis (other strand): A new viral RNA genome is made from the template produced in step 3. 6. Assembly: Viral RNA is surrounded by a protein coat. 7. Exit: The virus buds out of the cell, as spikes assemble on a piece of the host’s plasma membrane, which is now the viral envelope.
